data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The claim that a non-expert panel with a checklist is more reliable than a single expert is conditional: it holds only when the checklist encodes a causally complete or near-complete theory of the domain. In such cases, the panel's reliability gain is genuine because the checklist items mediate the outcome. However, in novel or complex domains where the checklist is incomplete, the expert's internal mutable theory will outperform the frozen checklist.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The domain is novel or rapidly evolving, such that the checklist's frozen theory is outdated or incomplete relative to the expert's current internal model.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The checklist items are surface correlates rather than causal mediators of the outcome, such that adversarial items break the checklist's predictive validity.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The expert's intuition incorporates information not captured by the checklist, leading to higher accuracy on atypical cases.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"A checklist functions as a 'frozen theory' encoding the checklist author's causal model. The panel executes this theory faithfully, while the expert executes their own internal, mutable theory. Reliability is determined by theory-quality \u00d7 execution-fidelity, not panel-vs-individual per se. When the frozen theory is causally complete, the panel's adherence is the mechanism of reliability; when it is incomplete, the expert's superior theory dominates.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
